frictionVectors.title: European gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains reliant on Algerian pipeline and LNG supplies, creating bargaining leverage but also pressure for expanded production and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya complicates border security and increases foreign competition for influence around Algeria's southern periphery.

frictionVectors.title: External control of strategic logistics
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor attracts US, European, and Chinese interest because of its route toward Copperbelt minerals, raising competition over infrastructure standards, financing, and access.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: Oil still dominates export earnings, leaving national fiscal sovereignty exposed to production declines, price shocks, and foreign technical and capital dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Cotonou corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Benin's port and trade routes remain exposed to shifting relations with Nigeria and the landlocked Sahel, while foreign investors seek influence over logistics infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel militant spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence near the northern borders threatens transport corridors, protected areas, and state access to mineral and agricultural zones.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market dependence
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains strong state leverage over diamonds, but weaker global demand and changing consumer behavior could reduce fiscal room and negotiating power.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: New interest in copper, lithium, and other minerals offers diversification but may create pressure for rapid concessions before local processing capacity is established.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector contestation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state control over gold through licensing and processing reforms, while informal production, smuggling, and armed-group taxation undermine oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security alignment
frictionVectors.details: Closer security cooperation with Russia reduces reliance on Western partners but introduces new external dependencies and uncertainty over the terms of resource-related engagement.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Burundi border tension
frictionVectors.details: Relations remain strained by accusations of support for armed actors linked to eastern DRC instability. Border restrictions and mistrust limit trade, security cooperation, and Burundi's regional bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-financed infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Road, energy, and mining projects depend heavily on external lenders and investors, leaving the state with limited control over financing terms and mineral value chains.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence at strategic ports
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport, and maritime-security infrastructure relies substantially on foreign capital and partnerships, creating long-term exposure to outside commercial and strategic priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Climate-linked resource vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Drought, water scarcity, and dependence on imported fuel and food constrain sovereign resilience despite strong institutions and relatively effective external-partnership management.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of extractive value chains
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, timber, and emerging mining projects remain dependent on foreign operators, financing, and export infrastructure, limiting domestic capture of value and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and transport disruption
frictionVectors.details: Separatist violence in the Northwest and Southwest continues to threaten roads, agricultural production, and project security. Instability raises the cost of state-led infrastructure and weakens territorial control.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security-for-access model
frictionVectors.details: The government's reliance on Russian-linked security assistance has strengthened regime protection while increasing outside influence over political decision-making and access to gold and diamond networks.

frictionVectors.title: Resource corridors remain insecure
frictionVectors.details: Weak roads, limited state administration, and armed-group activity obstruct formal mining and agricultural exports. Informal cross-border trade continues to divert value away from public institutions.

highlights: Oil revenue remains the fiscal anchor

frictionVectors.title: External security guarantees
frictionVectors.details: Chad's security posture remains tied to foreign military and intelligence partnerships as it manages threats from Sudan, Libya, and armed groups in the Lake Chad basin. This dependence narrows policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Oil infrastructure and revenue concentration
frictionVectors.details: Export pipelines, technical expertise, and financing remain externally linked, while state revenue is highly concentrated in hydrocarbons. Price shocks and opaque allocation of oil income create persistent sovereignty and governance risks.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and maritime sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to contest French control of Mayotte, while migration controls and maritime enforcement constrain Comorian sovereignty. France remains the decisive external actor in the archipelago.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and budget support rely heavily on France, Gulf donors, and multilateral lenders, limiting the government's room to set independent development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and copper bargaining power
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain a dominant position in industrial mining and processing, while Kinshasa seeks better contract terms and greater domestic value addition. Western and Gulf actors are competing for alternative access to critical minerals.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern security and supply corridors
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving armed groups and regional actors continues to disrupt borderland governance and mineral routes. External military, diplomatic, and commercial pressure narrows Kinshasa's effective control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues remain the foundation of fiscal stability, leaving Brazzaville vulnerable to price swings and foreign operators' technical and financial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese participation in roads, ports, and resource projects provides essential capacity but can constrain procurement autonomy and increase long-term repayment dependence.

highlights: Abidjan is becoming a regional logistics hub

frictionVectors.title: French and multinational influence
frictionVectors.details: France remains influential in finance, security, and major corporate networks, although Abidjan is diversifying toward Gulf, Chinese, and other international partners.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa and energy value capture
frictionVectors.details: The government is pushing local processing and stronger producer returns, but multinational trading power and dependence on imported energy still limit national control over value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military basing
frictionVectors.details: U.S., French, Chinese, Japanese, and other military presences provide revenue and security but make national sovereignty highly dependent on great-power competition and regional crises.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and port concentration
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed port and logistics infrastructure has expanded Djibouti's strategic relevance while increasing exposure to debt, lease disputes, and external control over critical transport assets.

highlights: Gulf and IMF capital deepen external leverage

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian control over Nile flows and seeks a binding operating agreement for the GERD. The dispute remains tied to wider Red Sea and Horn-of-Africa competition.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-asset financing
frictionVectors.details: IMF requirements and large Gulf investments provide liquidity but increase foreign influence over major land, port, and infrastructure decisions. Cairo retains substantial state control while trading autonomy for economic stabilization.

highlights: Hydrocarbon rents are entering a long decline
China remains a major infrastructure partner

frictionVectors.title: Oil depletion and opaque contracting
frictionVectors.details: Falling oil and gas output is shrinking fiscal space and intensifying competition over remaining concessions. Limited transparency leaves the state vulnerable to unfavorable terms and elite capture.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important for roads, ports, and public facilities. Debt exposure and weak diversification constrain Malabo's ability to convert infrastructure into broad-based sovereign capacity.

highlights: Red Sea geography magnifies strategic value
Mining remains central to hard-currency access

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to shipping lanes attract competing Gulf, Turkish, Egyptian, and other regional interests. Asmara guards its autonomy but faces pressure from broader Horn-of-Africa security alignments.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects provide scarce foreign exchange but expose the country to concentrated foreign operators and commodity-price swings. Limited transparency and sanctions-related scrutiny complicate long-term investment.

highlights: South African dependence anchors the economy

frictionVectors.title: Regional economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African trade, transport corridors, electricity links, and customs revenue. This provides stability but limits independent control over supply chains and fiscal policy.

frictionVectors.title: Taiwan-China diplomatic pressure
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini remains Taiwan's last formal diplomatic partner in Africa, making it a target for persistent Chinese diplomatic and economic pressure. Any shift would bring potential investment benefits but reduce strategic bargaining autonomy.

highlights: Port access is the central strategic vulnerability

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Landlocked Ethiopia remains dependent on neighboring states for maritime access, especially through Djibouti, while pursuing alternatives in the wider Red Sea region. Port diplomacy is entangled with tensions involving Somalia, Somaliland, Egypt, and Gulf powers.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure financing
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and foreign-exchange shortages constrain Addis Ababa's ability to finance transport, power, and industrial projects on sovereign terms. Chinese, Gulf, and multilateral capital can expand capacity while increasing external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: French Influence and Security Ties
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is recalibrating longstanding French political, military, and commercial influence while avoiding disruption to security cooperation and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Oil Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater state participation and local value addition in manganese and hydrocarbons, creating tension with established foreign operators and financiers.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Transport Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on regional transport links through Senegal, leaving trade and food-security logistics exposed to bilateral disputes and border disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Fisheries
frictionVectors.details: Limited monitoring capacity and opaque fishing arrangements leave domestic communities vulnerable to foreign fleet access and weak capture of marine-resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Gold Mining and Environmental Loss
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining continues to damage water systems and undermine formal state control, while powerful local and external trading networks capture substantial gold value.

frictionVectors.title: IMF Conditionality and Strategic Assets
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-supported reforms constrain policy space as Accra seeks to retain control over energy, minerals, and infrastructure assets.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Consortium and Infrastructure Control
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project binds Guinea to Chinese-linked and international partners for rail and port infrastructure, creating long-term risks around revenue capture and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Expansion and Local Displacement
frictionVectors.details: Rapid bauxite development generates foreign exchange but intensifies land, water, and community grievances while leaving Guinea dependent on external operators and export logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fisheries Access
frictionVectors.details: Weak maritime surveillance allows foreign fleets to capture significant value from Guinea-Bissau's waters, limiting domestic food security and public revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Senegal Border and Offshore Competition
frictionVectors.details: Maritime and offshore-resource issues with Senegal remain sensitive, while limited state capacity makes future oil and gas development vulnerable to unfavorable external deals.

frictionVectors.title: External financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service demands and negotiations with international lenders constrain Nairobi's fiscal autonomy. Chinese, Gulf, and Western partners compete for influence through infrastructure and budget support.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and northern corridor security
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu Port-South Sudan-Ethiopia corridor remains strategically important but commercially underdeveloped. Militancy, regional instability, and competing port interests limit Kenya's ability to convert infrastructure into sovereign leverage.

frictionVectors.title: South African water dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's fiscal position and infrastructure planning remain closely tied to water exports under the Lesotho Highlands Water Project. South Africa retains substantial negotiating and operational leverage over this strategic resource.

frictionVectors.title: Mining enclave vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Diamond revenues are concentrated among a small number of foreign-linked operators and exposed to volatile global prices. Limited domestic processing reduces local value capture and bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign mining concessions and rail access dominate Liberia's export model, generating revenue but limiting domestic control over logistics and processing. The government is under pressure to secure better local-content and fiscal terms.

frictionVectors.title: Monrovia port influence
frictionVectors.details: The port is central to Liberia's trade and security relationships, with outside partners seeking long-term commercial and strategic access. Weak infrastructure and institutional capacity constrain national oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Competing oil authorities
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks continue to contest control over the National Oil Corporation, export terminals, and budget flows. Production remains vulnerable to blockades and bargaining by armed groups.

frictionVectors.title: External military and energy leverage
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked actors, Egypt, the UAE, and European states retain influence through security partnerships, bases, migration policy, and energy interests. This external competition impedes unified resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and cobalt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led mining projects dominate Madagascar's nickel, cobalt, and mineral-export economy, while energy costs and infrastructure constraints reduce the state's negotiating leverage. Fiscal benefits remain vulnerable to commodity cycles and project disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Rare-earth and coastal resource competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Australian, European, and Gulf-linked interests are expanding attention to minerals, fisheries, ports, and logistics. Weak regulatory capacity raises risks of enclave development, environmental damage, and limited domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Mining concessions and revenue control
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is courting foreign investment in uranium, rare earths, graphite, and other minerals while seeking stronger local value capture. Limited state capacity and fiscal dependence could leave the government with weak bargaining leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and transport vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Fuel shortages, foreign-exchange constraints, and dependence on imported energy continue to expose Malawi to external price shocks. Reliance on regional corridors and donor-backed infrastructure limits strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is renegotiating mining terms and asserting greater state participation, particularly in gold. Disputes with foreign operators risk reduced investment, litigation, and production disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security and infrastructure dependency
frictionVectors.details: Mali's reliance on Russian security support has displaced several Western partnerships but has not resolved insurgent threats. Attacks on roads, power infrastructure, and mining zones continue to undermine sovereign control of resources.

highlights: Iron ore and green-hydrogen ambitions advance

frictionVectors.title: GTA gas-project dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers Mauritania new export revenue and diplomatic weight, but offshore production remains dependent on foreign operators, technology, and cross-border coordination.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and corridor concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore exports remain tied to the SNIM rail and port system, while future green-hydrogen projects depend heavily on external capital and European demand. Concentrated infrastructure creates exposure to market and security disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos sovereignty and strategic alignment
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius continues pursuing sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago while balancing relations with the United Kingdom, United States, and India. The issue constrains room for maneuver over Indian Ocean security and maritime access.

frictionVectors.title: Port and financial-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius seeks to expand port, bunkering, and logistics activity with external partners, especially India, while preserving its international financial role. Competition, compliance demands, and dependence on imported energy limit autonomous leverage.

highlights: Western Sahara remains strategic fault line

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses phosphate, fisheries, renewable-energy, and port projects in Western Sahara to reinforce its territorial claim. Polisario opposition and legal challenges from European actors remain persistent external pressure points.

frictionVectors.title: Industrial supply-chain balancing
frictionVectors.details: Automotive, battery, solar, and port investments deepen ties with the European Union, China, Gulf states, and the United States. This diversification strengthens Morocco's leverage but creates exposure to competing foreign strategic agendas.

highlights: Cabo Delgado Remains the Sovereignty Test

frictionVectors.title: Rovuma LNG Dependence
frictionVectors.details: International energy majors and foreign lenders retain decisive influence over the timing, financing, and operating terms of northern LNG projects. Delays and cost escalation continue to limit Mozambique's near-term control over expected gas revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to threaten communities, transport corridors, and energy infrastructure. Government forces and external security partners remain essential to protecting strategic projects.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Strategic Projects
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale hydrogen, uranium, oil, and critical-mineral projects require substantial external capital and technology. Namibia is strengthening local-content and state-participation demands, but financing needs constrain its negotiating leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Logistics and Export Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Limited rail, port, water, and electricity capacity could leave Namibia dependent on foreign infrastructure partners and neighboring transit routes. Expansion around Walvis Bay is strategically important but capital intensive.

highlights: Pipeline and Uranium Access at Risk

frictionVectors.title: Oil Export Corridor Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Niger's crude exports depend on cross-border pipeline infrastructure and stable relations with coastal neighbors. Political rupture, sanctions, and insecurity can redirect value away from Niamey despite stronger formal state control.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Security Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The junta is reducing Western influence over uranium and security cooperation while seeking alternative partners. This creates uncertainty over mining operations, revenue flows, and the protection of extraction sites.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Refinery Dependence
frictionVectors.details: New domestic refining capacity could reduce import dependence, but upstream investment, technology, and trading networks remain heavily internationalized. Fiscal stress limits Abuja's ability to capture the full value of its hydrocarbons.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Pipeline Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Theft, sabotage, and armed disruption in the Niger Delta continue to erode public revenues and weaken state control over production corridors. Security contracting and community bargaining remain central to infrastructure protection.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Mineral Scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's role as a regional minerals hub faces sustained international scrutiny over supply chains linked to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Sanctions or tighter traceability rules could affect exports, investment, and diplomatic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: External Security and Aid Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda maintains substantial strategic autonomy, but its regional security posture and development model remain exposed to Western aid, Gulf investment, and international political pressure. Tensions with the DRC and donors can directly affect logistics and market access.

frictionVectors.title: UNCERTAIN OFFSHORE HYDROCARBONS
frictionVectors.details: Prospective Gulf of Guinea blocks attract foreign interest, but limited discoveries and weak domestic capacity constrain São Tomé and Príncipe's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Ports, energy, and connectivity depend heavily on external finance and partnerships, creating long-term leverage risks for a small island state.

highlights: New oil and gas era begins
Resource sovereignty moves to the center

frictionVectors.title: CONTRACT RENEGOTIATION PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater national control and revenue capture from hydrocarbons, risking friction with foreign operators and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND FOREIGN FLEETS
frictionVectors.details: Competition over fishing access, especially involving distant-water fleets, continues to test enforcement capacity and coastal community trust.

frictionVectors.title: STRATEGIC PORT COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles is balancing security and infrastructure ties with India, China, and Western partners while protecting its autonomy over maritime facilities.

frictionVectors.title: TOURISM AND DEBT EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Heavy dependence on tourism and imported infrastructure leaves the economy vulnerable to external shocks and creditor influence.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONCESSION LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects rely on foreign capital, leaving the state exposed to disputes over royalties, local content, and environmental costs.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed transport corridors improve export capacity but can lock national infrastructure into the priorities of external mining and logistics firms.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE OIL ALIGNMENTS
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed exploration and licensing are advancing faster than Somalia's ability to establish unified federal-state governance and transparent revenue sharing.

frictionVectors.title: PORTS AND SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, and other external actors provide critical military and infrastructure support, strengthening state capacity while competing for strategic access.

highlights: Power and rail bottlenecks constrain autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Minerals and strategic investment
frictionVectors.details: South Africa retains substantial regulatory control over platinum, manganese and chromium, but depends on foreign capital, technology and export markets. Competition among China, the United States, Europe and Gulf investors is increasing political pressure over critical-mineral partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and freight infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortfalls, port congestion and deteriorating rail capacity weaken domestic control over resource value chains. External lenders and private operators are increasingly relevant to infrastructure recovery.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-export corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on pipelines and export infrastructure crossing Sudan, leaving national revenue exposed to conflict, sabotage and bargaining by external authorities. Chinese-linked oil interests remain influential alongside regional diplomatic pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-group and regional influence
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation and insecurity limit state control over oil-producing areas and transport routes. Uganda, Sudan and other regional actors retain significant leverage over security and political outcomes.

highlights: Gold and ports attract rival patrons

frictionVectors.title: Gold war economy
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling provide financing to armed actors while reducing transparent state revenue. Regional traders and foreign networks benefit from weak oversight and competing claims to mining zones.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Port access, logistics facilities and prospective mineral routes are subjects of competition among Gulf states, Russia-linked interests and regional powers. The civil war prevents Khartoum from exercising consistent sovereign control over these assets.

highlights: Ports and gas reshape strategic leverage

frictionVectors.title: LNG and mining negotiations
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking greater domestic value capture from natural gas and mining while still requiring international capital and technical expertise. Contract terms and local-content demands remain points of friction with multinational investors.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of Dar es Salaam and central transport corridors increases Tanzania's leverage over regional trade, but also draws competition from Kenya, Gulf investors and China. Financing and operating arrangements could affect long-term control of strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé strengthens Togo's regional position, but its expansion depends heavily on foreign capital, operators and shipping networks. External commercial influence may limit the state's ability to fully control strategic logistics decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate remains a core national resource, yet production, financing and export performance are exposed to international commodity conditions and technical partnerships. Government efforts to retain value are constrained by infrastructure and investment needs.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration and Financing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: European funding and political engagement remain closely tied to migration control, limiting Tunisian bargaining autonomy. Fiscal stress increases reliance on external partners without fully resolving debt and investment constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Algerian Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains dependent on Algerian gas and electricity flows, leaving key energy infrastructure vulnerable to regional politics. Domestic production and renewable expansion have not yet eliminated this structural exposure.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP and Western Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline binds national revenue prospects to foreign operators, lenders, and export infrastructure. Environmental criticism and Western pressure compete with Kampala's determination to retain control over its petroleum strategy.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important across transport, energy, and industrial projects. Debt-service obligations and opaque contracting can narrow Uganda's policy room while increasing strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is leveraging competition among Chinese, Western, and Gulf investors to attract capital into copper and cobalt. However, foreign ownership, export concentration, and uncertain local-processing capacity still limit domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Fiscal Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Efforts to raise mining revenues and improve contract transparency risk conflict with major international operators. Power shortages and transport bottlenecks further weaken Zambia's negotiating position.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium Processing and Ownership
frictionVectors.details: Harare is restricting unprocessed mineral exports to capture more value from lithium and other strategic resources. Limited domestic capital and technology nevertheless leave the sector heavily reliant on Chinese and other foreign investors.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Sanctions Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages, sanctions-related financial restrictions, and weak infrastructure raise operating costs across mining and manufacturing. These pressures push Zimbabwe toward alternative external partners while reducing its ability to enforce favorable terms.
